Reductive amination is a chemical reaction in which a carbonyl compound (such as an aldehyde or ketone) is converted into an amine by reacting it with an amine or ammonia in the presence of a reducing agent. This process is widely used in organic synthesis to form carbon-nitrogen bonds, which are common in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and other fine chemicals.

The general reaction can be represented as follows:

\[ \text{R-CO-R'} + \text{R''-NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{R-CH(NR'')-R'} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \]

Where:
- R-CO-R' represents the carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone).
- R''-NH2 represents the amine or ammonia.
- R-CH(NR'')-R' represents the resulting amine product.
- H2O is water, a byproduct of the reaction.

The reducing agent used in the reaction can vary, but common choices include sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH3CN), sodium triacetoxyborohydride (NaBH(OAc)3), and sodium borohydride (NaBH4). The choice of reducing agent can affect the selectivity and efficiency of the reaction, as well as the conditions under which the reaction is carried out.

Reductive amination is a versatile method for the synthesis of amines and is particularly useful for the preparation of complex molecules where the direct formation of a carbon-nitrogen bond is required.
